P1.text: Code overlap does not explain forgetting under the error-driven rule (r = 0.27 over 14 sparsity-wiring points). Comparing classes by normalised weights without a bias term cuts forgetting by 0.17 on average and up to 0.29, so recency bias dominates. The associative readout, which normalises by construction, forgets 0.05.

P2.text: Two-shape classes peak at sparsity 0.01 (Dense random projection), 0.02 (Measured PN→KC).

P3.text: Dense random codes follow the exact overlap curve (RMSE 0.028); measured wiring deviates (RMSE 0.098, mean bias -0.074).

P4.text: Capacity extrapolated from 10 classes to 400: mean error 0.102 at f = 0.01, mean error 0.049 at f = 0.05, mean error 0.017 at f = 0.2. The prediction is optimistic everywhere (signed error +0.102, +0.049, -0.005) and worst for the sparsest codes, where wrong-class scores are right-skewed (skew +0.71 at f = 0.01, +0.25 at f = 0.05, -0.01 at f = 0.2) rather than the Gaussian the model assumes.

note: Single-seed model tests. Verdict thresholds (recency drop > 0.05, interior peak, RMSE < 0.05, mean error < 0.08) are set in theory.py. P1 originally predicted that forgetting would track code overlap; the simulation refuted it and the test now compares the two candidate mechanisms instead.
